KEY MESSAGE 1... 
The familiar pattern remains this morning 
characterized by a broad mid/upper trough over south central Canada 
and the northern Plains into the Great Lakes and a broad mid/upper 
ridge over the Desert Southwest and southern Plains. This is keeping 
active WNW mid/upper flow in place across the southern Great Lakes 
and Ohio Valley overtop a quasi-stationary east-west front. 

The next in the train of reinforcing shortwaves is moving into 
western Ohio early this morning. RAP analysis hints at a weak 
surface wave tied to this mid/upper shortwave that is traversing the 
frontal boundary, and the boundary is retreating northward this 
morning in response. Weak warm air/theta e advection and 500-1000 
joules of MLCAPE in the presence of a very moist environment is 
triggering a large area of convection along the slowly retreating 
front this morning. This is being aided by upper diffluence and mid-
level PVA, so expect showers and thunderstorms to be widespread 
again this morning as they slowly lift east and northeast. Given 
PWATs near 2 inches, skinny CAPE, and high freezing levels with deep 
warm cloud layers, torrential rainfall will accompany the 
convection, so will need to monitor for localized flooding this 
morning, particularly if heavy rain occurs in spots that saw it 
yesterday. Much of the lakeshore from Erie and Lorain Counties 
through central and southern Cuyahoga County measured 1 to 3 inches 
of rain since Thursday night, so these areas will be vulnerable if 
the convection can build farther north this morning.

This morning activity will exit NW PA by about 14Z, and expect a 
lull with quite a bit of sunshine into this afternoon allowing 
temperatures to warm into the mid/upper 80s ahead of the trailing 
cold front. This front is trending a few hours slower since it 
parallels the mid/upper flow but should sink across the region this 
evening. Pooling low-level moisture along the boundary (dew points 
70-75 F) beneath a plume of steeper mid-level lapse rates around 7 
C/Km will combine with the surface heating to yield strong 
instability this afternoon and evening. RAP and NAM forecast 
soundings suggest near 3000 joules of MLCAPE will be possible by mid 
to late afternoon, and with just enough deep layer effective shear 
for loose convective organization (0-6 Km shear around 25 knots), 
could see a few strong to severe storms with damaging winds late 
this afternoon and evening. The main question is convective 
coverage. Forecast soundings show quite a bit of dry air, and while 
this could aid downburst potential (DCAPE near 1000 joules), it may 
be too dry to get a lot of storm coverage. The thinking is that 
there will be a broken line of convection that will move ESE across 
the area in the 21-03Z timeframe, with a few widely scattered cells 
possible ahead of the line.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Weak surface high pressure will briefly build in 
tonight and Sunday, pushing the front to near the Ohio River and 
allowing somewhat less humid air to filter in (dew points in the 
low/mid 60s), however, the front will retreat back north as a warm 
front Sunday night in response to a much more potent mid/upper 
shortwave dropping into the Upper Midwest. This will bring the rich 
low-level moisture back into the region for Sunday night and Monday 
and possibly fuel an organized severe weather and heavy rainfall 
event.

Confidence continues to be low in terms of how convection will play 
out Sunday night through Monday night, so this set up has a 
high ceiling but also high bust potential. As the potent 
shortwave drops into the Upper Midwest Sunday evening, a 30-40 
knot low-level jet and northeast periphery of a stout EML 
should trigger a severe MCS that will propagate ESE into 
northern Illinois, northern Indiana, and Lower Michigan along 
the strong instability gradient. This MCS will be outrunning the
best instability and upper support by the time it reaches 
northern Ohio overnight Sunday night, but instability will be 
slowly increasing as the frontal boundary retreats north, so 
expect it to affect northern Ohio in some fashion Sunday night, 
with potential for gusty winds and heavy downpours. Best chance 
for this will be in NW Ohio. The bigger impact from this MCS 
will be how it affects convective redevelopment Monday. The 
shortwave is expected to continue east across the central and 
southern Great Lakes Monday with a resultant increase in mid- 
level flow yielding 40-50 knots of deep layer effective shear. 
This mid-level jet will encourage a low-level jet response by 
Monday evening to possibly ignite a new MCS over southern Lower 
Michigan, Lake Erie, and northern Ohio ahead of a cold front,

much cloud debris and showers from Sunday night linger into
